statements.quote: Obvious things you can win a fight about: Under the accountable care act, there are rules about network sufficiency.
statements.context: ERISA fiduciary-duty essay (post dated 2023-06-24). The author asserts that plan members can win disputes with employer health plans over ACA network-sufficiency rules, notably the 10-day maximum wait for an outpatient mental health appointment.
statements.note: Borderline: a legal-outcome claim ('you can win') rather than a dated forecast.

statements.quote: In states with bans on gender-affirming care, the wait time for an appointment for your child’s gender dysphoria, assessment, or treatment, is now infinite
statements.context: Example of a network-sufficiency breach: in states that ban gender-affirming care (Texas, Florida, Utah, Arkansas named), the author says no appointment will be available. Footnote 5 adds 'until Governor Gregory Abbott is run out of town on a rail' and that there probably are no gender-affirming care visits available in Texas.
statements.note: Rhetorical, hyperbolic present-tense claim with an open-ended future reading; borderline.

statements.quote: Your employer needs to get compliant. And they’re probably going to call their Benefits Broker.
statements.context: Under the heading 'The Covering Of @&$ Begins.': predicted employer reaction to the 2021 ERISA fiduciary-duty rules. Employers will seek compliance and turn to their benefits brokers.
statements.note: Behavioral prediction about employers; first sentence is normative, second predictive.

statements.quote: It is in the interests of those parties to file suit to cover their own liability, too.
statements.context: Same passage: the author implies that employers and their benefits brokers will themselves file suit to cover their ERISA fiduciary liability.
statements.note: Incentive claim with an implicit prediction of litigation; borderline.

statements.quote: At a bare minimum, they’re probably going to want to buy a compliant plan during the next enrollment cycle.
statements.context: Employers under ERISA will move to compliant health plans at the next enrollment cycle, or go self-funded and check compliance with a tool like the Health Rosetta Plan Grader.

statements.quote: And if ERISA wasn’t bad enough, I suspect Perez v. Sturgis will be applied for damages under ADA next.
statements.context: Legal forecast near the end of the essay: the Supreme Court decision Perez v. Sturgis will next be used to seek damages under the Americans with Disabilities Act in health-plan disputes.

statements.quote: Health Plans— the new Lawyer Employment Act of 2023!
statements.context: Joke line directly after the Perez v. Sturgis call: the author expects a wave of litigation against employer health plans in 2023.
statements.note: Satirical phrasing; the underlying expectation of a litigation surge reads as sincere.

statements.quote: These are different motives, and won’t be universally appealing.
statements.context: Contrasting the author's own disclosure motives with Rick Doblin's politically expedient choice of PTSD as MAPS's indication; the author predicts Doblin's motives and messaging will not appeal universally.
statements.note: Weak, general reception claim; borderline.

statements.quote: The more therapists who are exposed to the biasing experience of psychedelic treatment the fewer of them will have as much doubt as will be useful some of the time . Some of the time, they will not help.
statements.context: Closing argument against Doblin's proposal that all MDMA therapists take MDMA: more exposed therapists means less useful clinical doubt, and psychedelic treatments will fail some of the time.
statements.note: Compound: a dose-response claim about therapist bias plus a general 'treatments will sometimes fail' claim.

statements.quote: When more friends use your referral link to subscribe (free or paid), you’ll receive special benefits.
statements.context: Substack referral-program announcement for The Frontier Psychiatrists: a 1-month comp for 3 referrals, 3 months for 5, 6 months for 25.
statements.note: Own-newsletter program terms; trivial commitment. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: So the article I'm going to post on the first is a reader favorite from the past year of writing.
statements.context: Item 1 ('The Year in Review') of the author's 'what is cooking' list of upcoming articles: a reader-favorites retrospective to be posted on 1 July 2023, one year after he took over the newsletter.
statements.note: Own publishing plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: This pending article concerns pharmacy benefit managers, payment models, and big Healthcare.
statements.context: Item 2 ('Soprano RX.') of the upcoming-articles list: a pending piece comparing the double-speak of American healthcare economics and PBMs to the mafia code of omerta.
statements.note: Own publishing plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: This is a challenging piece to write. It’s about a personal experience, young love, confusion, and dealing with the fallout from child abuse. I’m taking my time.
statements.context: Item 3 ('Nothing was Easy') of the upcoming-articles list: a personal narrative piece in progress for about two weeks.
statements.note: Own publishing plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Psychedelic exceptionalism needs to stop , or it will get in the way of psychedelic medicine being actual medicine .
statements.context: Item 4 ('Dear Psychedelic Exceptionalism') setup: conditional claim that psychedelic exceptionalism, if it continues, will obstruct psychedelic medicine from becoming accepted, regulated medicine.
statements.note: Conditional forecast about the psychedelic field; first clause is normative ('needs to stop'), second clause predictive.

statements.quote: This article is a little bit more lighthearted. It's not done yet.
statements.context: Item 4 ('Dear Psychedelic Exceptionalism') of the upcoming-articles list: a follow-up article on psychedelic exceptionalism, unfinished at time of writing.
statements.note: Own publishing plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: I am taking apart the argument I've made in different formats about how Dobbs, as a decision, creates turmoil regarding privacy regulations and how I see it playing out as it relates to the standards around privacy federally.
statements.context: Item 5 ('Cerebral class action fanfiction') of the upcoming-articles list: a planned piece using a case against Cerebral as a hook for how the Dobbs decision will play out for federal privacy standards.
entities: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization
statements.note: Publishing plan that embeds an implicit forecast (Dobbs will create turmoil in federal privacy regulation); compound. CONTROL candidate for the plan part.

statements.quote: I've worked on writing this; I'm not sure I will get to publish it. Not anytime soon.
statements.context: Item 6 ('How to Never Work in This Town Again') of the upcoming-articles list: a story from the author's training years that he doubts he will publish.
statements.note: Own publishing plan, hedged negative; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: If I am telling you it is offensive, other people are just quietly making sure your interventions don't go anywhere.
statements.context: Whimsical essay against demanding that all psychedelic therapists take the drugs. The author warns that the exceptionalist attitude alienates gatekeepers who will quietly block psychedelic interventions.
statements.note: Implicit prediction that psychedelic interventions will be blocked by alienated stakeholders; borderline.

statements.quote: We don’t need an insufferable counter-culture nu-Phish concert in an unconvincing Phrma cos-play scene that drags on endlessly till the FDA takes it down for being a Bad Ad.
statements.context: Closing line: the author warns that psychedelic counter-culture promotion dressed up as pharma will eventually draw FDA enforcement (the Bad Ad program) if it continues.
statements.horizon_text: till the FDA takes it down
statements.note: Satirical framing (author labels the post 'whimsy being used to make a serious point'); the FDA-enforcement expectation reads as a sincere warning.

statements.quote: Please keep reading and subscribing and I will keep writing.
statements.context: One-year anniversary post (2023-07-01); the author commits to keep writing the daily newsletter.
statements.note: Trivial own commitment; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Please share the living daylights out of this, and in the next year we will be launching more advertising for things I think are a good idea?
statements.context: Anniversary post: plan to launch more advertising in the newsletter over the coming year.
statements.note: Own business plan; the trailing question mark softens it. CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: subscribe, and I promise everything will be all right.
statements.context: Footnote tagline of a reassurance column about the fear of 'going crazy'.
statements.note: Joke subscription tagline; no real expectation.

statements.quote: The vibrancy and appeal have the flavor of an FDIC press release before an old-fashioned bank runs.
statements.context: Act I: after 555 unfilled emergency medicine residency spots in the 2023 Match (up from 219 in 2022), the author likens ACEP's reassuring statement to a bank regulator's statement before a run, implying the EM residency pipeline is heading for collapse.
statements.note: Implicit forecast by analogy; direction (worsening EM match) is clear, magnitude is not.

statements.quote: Furthermore, extrapolating current trends, we anticipate the EP workforce could be 20-30% oversupplied by 2030.
statements.context: Quoted 2020 academic workforce projection that emergency physicians (EPs) would be oversupplied by 2030; the author cites it to mock it in light of the 2023 Match.
statements.note: Third-party forecast (2020 EM workforce study) that the author disputes.

statements.quote: Rarely do we read more damning words than “conservative estimate”— it is the academic version of Jim Cramer’s telling you Silicon Valley Bank is a top 10-pick in February 2023.
statements.context: The author's response to the 2020 projection of a 20-30% EM physician oversupply by 2030: he compares it to Jim Cramer's SVB pick just before that bank failed, implying the oversupply forecast will prove badly wrong (shortage, not surplus).
statements.note: Implicit negative call on a third-party forecast; the author's own expectation is an EM physician shortfall rather than oversupply by 2030.

statements.quote: The crucial point to understand about private equity investment, specifically in healthcare: is that it is a scam for the rest of us, and maybe for their investors too. It can’t generate value . The timeline is too short.
statements.context: Act II: the author argues that PE's 3-7 year hold period cannot produce real health value, so PE healthcare deals will fail to create value and may burn investors. Footnote 4: 2-4 years is enough for balance-sheet sleight of hand, not for improving health. American Physician Partners is the example.
statements.note: Structural claim with predictive implication (PE healthcare investments will not create value; investor losses possible).

statements.quote: The 2023 Match should terrify us all.
statements.context: Act III close: the author frames the 2023 emergency medicine Match collapse as a warning about the future of emergency care staffing (not enough physicians in ERs).
statements.note: Warning framed with 'should'; the predictive reading (worsening emergency care) is implicit. Borderline.

statements.quote: The risks that keep doctors accountable can also limit private equity investors, possibly deterring them from meddling in medicine.
statements.context: Act IV proposal: if corporate-practice-of-medicine violations carried personal liability for executives, like license risk for doctors, that could deter private equity from healthcare.
statements.note: Conditional policy prediction tied to a normative proposal.

statements.quote: If you do, I’ll comp you a subscription for a year.
statements.context: Parody podcast episode blurb: the author promises a one-year complimentary subscription to listeners who leave a five-star review on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.
statements.note: Trivial conditional own commitment; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: I suspect there is a shared neural basis for both.
statements.context: Explanatory piece on OCPD versus OCD; the author hypothesizes a shared neural basis for the two conditions.
statements.note: Scientific hypothesis about present neurobiology, not a forecast; logged for recall.

statements.quote: We are approaching the “leftover loss threshold.” We are closer and closer to the asymptote of unbelievable suffering in our experience.
statements.context: Essay on the 'mental health crisis' as a crisis of hopelessness. Using the TV show The Leftovers (2% of people vanish, 2000/100,000) as an 'unimaginable loss' benchmark, the author says US death and despair rates (2021 death rate 1043/100,000; considering-suicide estimate 4015/100,000) are approaching that threshold.
statements.note: Trend claim implying the threshold will be reached; borderline.

statements.quote: Those attempts will turn into completed suicides later. We don’t know which ones.
statements.context: Discussing CDC youth suicide-attempt data: since attempted suicide is the best predictor of completed suicide, the author predicts that today's attempts will become completed suicides later.
statements.note: Epidemiological prediction; directional at population level, not falsifiable per individual.

statements.quote: And it's only going in the wrong direction
statements.context: On gun violence (Gun Violence Archive interactive map) after the June 23 Supreme Court ruling making guns more accessible and the Parkland survivors' protests: the author says gun violence is trending worse.
statements.note: Present-progressive trend claim with an implicit forward reading; borderline.

statements.quote: It is not stopping. Our hearts will be ground into the dirt.
statements.context: Footnote 1 of the mental-health-crisis essay: the author predicts the wave of suicide, overdose and gun deaths, and the grief it causes, will continue.
statements.note: Bleak general prediction; low specificity.
